title: Coral Atolls
objective: After this level you can explain how ring-shaped atolls form.
summary: A reef around a sinking volcano keeps growing up until only a ring around a lagoon remains. Darwin reasoned it out; drilling at Enewetak in 1952 found the buried volcano.

cards.headline: Darwin explained coral atolls before he'd seen a true coral reef.
cards.body: He worked it out on the west coast of South America, during the Beagle voyage, while thinking about how land slowly rises and sinks. His answer to the riddle of ring-shaped islands: look for the volcano that isn't there anymore.

events.label: A fringing reef grows straight out from the shore of a volcanic island
The island sinks and the reef keeps growing: now a barrier reef beyond a lagoon
The island sinks out of sight, leaving a ring of reef around a lagoon: an atoll

cards.headline: Where did the island go?
cards.body: Remember Level 64: old volcanic islands sink under their own weight. Darwin's insight was that the reef doesn't have to go down with the ship. It keeps growing upward while the island sinks, so it stays near the surface as the volcano disappears below. It's slow work: barrier reefs and atolls can take from 100,000 to 30 million years to fully form.

cards.fact: In 1952, drills at Enewetak Atoll went through more than 1 km of coral before hitting volcanic rock.
cards.context: It was the first geologic drilling of an atoll, and it found the sunken volcano right where Darwin's idea said it should be. He had published his theory in 1842, so the proof took more than a century to arrive. Worth the wait.

cards.headline: Where the race is lost
cards.body: An atoll is a race: coral grows up while the island sinks. At the far northwest end of the Hawaiian chain sits Kure Atoll, the northernmost coral atoll in the world. There, cooler water slows the coral until its growth only just matches the sinking. Past Kure, the reefs can't keep up, and the chain carries on as drowned, submerged platforms. Scientists call this tipping line the Darwin Point.

cards.headline: Atolls: explained
learned: Fringing reef, barrier reef, then atoll
The reef grows up as the island sinks
Past Kure Atoll, reefs lose the race

questions.prompt: In Darwin's model, what is left once the volcanic island has sunk out of sight?

options.label: A bare volcanic cone at sea level
options.rationale: The volcano has sunk below the surface.

options.label: A fringing reef along a new shore
options.rationale: That's the first stage, not the last.

options.label: A barrier reef across from the land
options.rationale: That's the middle stage, while land still shows.

options.label: A ring of reef around a lagoon

questions.explanation: When the island sinks out of sight, the reef that kept growing upward is left as a ring around a lagoon: an atoll.

questions.prompt: Why was the 1952 drilling at Enewetak Atoll strong evidence for Darwin's idea?

options.label: It hit volcanic rock under more than 1 km of coral
It showed the atoll was floating on the sea
options.rationale: Atolls sit on sunken volcanoes, not floating.

options.label: It found coral all the way down with no bottom
options.rationale: The drill reached volcanic rock beneath the coral.

options.label: It proved the lagoon was a meteorite crater
options.rationale: The drill found a volcano, as Darwin predicted.

questions.explanation: Darwin predicted a sunken volcano under every atoll; the drill found volcanic rock beneath more than 1 km of coral.

questions.prompt: From Level 43: reef corals need sunlight for their algae. Why does an atoll's reef keep growing upward as its island sinks?

options.label: Its coral feeds on heat from the volcano
options.rationale: Reef corals depend on sunlight reaching their algae.

options.label: It stays near the sunlit surface
Coral grows fastest in deep, dark water
options.rationale: Light fades with depth, and reef builders need it.

options.label: The sinking island pushes the reef upward
options.rationale: The reef grows up on its own while the island sinks.

questions.explanation: The reef keeps growing upward while the island sinks, so it stays near the surface, where light reaches the algae that feed reef corals.
